transcript.text: This is the ascent portion of our mission.
On the countdown of the Cape just went flawlessly.
We were really pleased with the way things went down.
Went on down there.
The engine's starting.
You can see the shock waves come out of the throat to the nozzles.
The nozzles vibrate.
The engines get up and stable in about six seconds.
Solid rocket motor's fire and we're off.
For a new guy doing this the first time,
it's really a thrill and that thing feels like being on a rough train while the solid rocket motors are firing.
If you all have been on a rough railroad track,
that's about what it feels like.
It's a very interesting ride.
You can function normally.
Right before we lifted off, Crip said get ready for the ride of your lives and he was right.
It's the ride of your life.
It's still a big throw on your third time.
One of the neat things about this mission was we're going to do direct insertion into orbit.
We didn't do an orbital maneuvering system one burn right after the main engine's cut off.
We're going right into orbit off the pad and we're going up 250 miles so the trajectory and everything is a little bit different.
It made a real interesting ride out of it.
The solid rocket motors, the engines and everything just are magnificent.
We didn't have a glitch the whole ascent which is really nice.
You don't want any glitches when this kind of stuff's going on outside your window.
We all kept on watching Crip make sure this is the way it's always supposed to be.
Solid rocket motors separated.
They saw the plumes from the separation motors.
Those fog up our windows pretty good up in front.
They put a haze on the forward windows when they go off.
You get a nice flash in the windows but it's a nice smooth separation.
This is our external tank coming in by Hawaii.
One of our test objectives was to put that tank in so they could take pictures of it.
This is the tank breaking up just south of Hawaii.
It's low light TV so you get some blooming in it but you can also see the rather large pieces of the tank and how much is broken up.
They were trying to measure the footprint of those pieces as they came into the ocean to see how big the dispersion was on them.
That's all bits and pieces of the tank we carry.
It lit up the area pretty good over there.
This next picture is the orbiter coming right along behind.
If it hadn't been for the alms burn we'd been right behind the tank which we didn't want to do.
This next series goes to each of the guys to make sure you prove that we're on board which we were.
Some of our going through our little activities and getting squared away.
A shot shows the box with the Lindhof camera we had on board.
First down we've flown that.
Got a 5 inch by 4 inch square format that really makes some nice pictures that takes this coast picture we saw a while ago we shot from that.
DJ?
On day two we started a sequence of RMS activities that would result in the deploy of LDF.
I can't say enough about our Canadian friends that built and designed the RMS just a beautiful flying hardware.
This is the starboard grapple fixture of LDF that we used for the deploy.

Essentially the payload is tied down in the bay with some latches and once the RMS has it securely grappled the grip released the latches and we pulled it out and put it through its paces for a couple of hours.
Very steadily poised the orbiter and the right attitude and released the payload rates.
LDF is unique and it is a very simple payload.
No gyroscopes or anything like that nature on board and it was incumbent upon us to release it without tipping it or getting any kind of motion started.
We hope the next 10 months to a year it will stay in this exact attitude that we left it in for recovering.
We also carried a unique camera on board that is referred to as iMacs that shoots a 70mm movie film and here it shows a scene with me loading the magazine and running it through.
It is about a thousand feet of film in a mag.
Did you think?

Every time it was on the big deck I was in the bag but that is what we used to change the film out from the can into the magazine.

We made the rendezvous without any problem at all.
This is that in the bay and the MMU getting ready to take off for the satellite.
See the teapads sticking out there in front.

But all that felt very comfortable from my standpoint of watching the satellite and watching Pinkie do the fly over just like we planned it.
It is a nice stable device that the MMU really performed superbly throughout the flight.
The MMU was really a very nice machine to fly. You could put it wherever you wanted.
Flying up on the satellite was just like we had done in the simulator.
All the way up to the point here where we attempt to do a dock and a teapad hits that little pin that is sticking out and bounces right off.
That is a view from the helmet mounted camera.
The satellite initially was rotating at about the 9th of a degree per second about its long axis before the attempts to grapple it.
This I think is the last attempt I made at doing the docking.
We had some pretty good rates on the satellite already.
So you go in there and I'll launch on bounce right out again and bounce out at about the same rate you go in.

because I didn't have any reason to think it would work any better.
We did have a rotating grapple up our sleeve however the satellite was tumbling in over in as you can see here.

So we brought Pinkie back in and attempted to go ahead and grapple it however when we went back it actually developed more of a tumble again.

So we elected to go ahead and go along with that option and backed out and to try again another day.
